name: Soldering
title: Tools, joints, flux and rework
intro: Soldering joins metal parts with a fusible alloy. These lessons cover tools, through-hole technique, flux, how to recognise good and bad joints, ESD care, desoldering and practical rework tips. Irons are hot; fumes need ventilation; eye protection is not optional.

lessons.title: Soldering tools
lessons.summary: Iron, tip, stand, sponge/brass and solder.

sections.p: A temperature-controlled soldering iron (often 300–370 °C for electronics solder) with interchangeable tips is the core tool. Use a stand; never leave a hot iron loose on the bench. Warning: tips cause instant burns.
Chisel and conical tips cover most through-hole work. Keep the tip tinned (shiny with solder). Clean on brass wool or a damp sponge — brass wool is gentler on plating.

Electronics solder is usually a tin-based alloy, sometimes with lead (Pb) in older/some hobby stock, often lead-free (e.g. SAC305) in modern work. Use resin/flux-cored solder for electronics — never acid plumbing flux on circuits.
Helping hands, tweezers, flush cutters, fume extraction or a fan out a window, and safety glasses round out a starter kit.
Work ventilated. Wash hands after handling leaded solder. Unplug irons when finished. Keep cords from snagging the iron off the stand.

lessons.title: Through-hole soldering
lessons.summary: Heat the joint, feed solder, inspect.

sections.p: Through-hole parts have leads that pass through PCB pads. The reliable method: heat the pad and the lead together with the iron tip, then feed solder into the hot joint — not onto the iron alone.

1) Insert and secure the part. 2) Touch tip to pad+lead. 3) Feed solder opposite the tip so it flows onto both metals. 4) Remove solder, then iron. 5) Let it cool without moving. 6) Trim leads with cutters — eye protection on.
A few seconds of good contact beats ten seconds of a dirty cold tip. Too much heat lifts pads; too little makes cold joints. Practice on scrap boards.
A stable board (vice or helping hands) frees both hands for iron and solder. Wobbly joints become bad joints.

lessons.title: Flux and wetting
lessons.summary: Cleaning oxides so solder can flow.

sections.p: Flux chemically cleans oxides so molten solder can wet the metal — spread and bond instead of beading up. Cored solder already contains flux; extra liquid or paste flux helps rework and stubborn joints.

Good wetting looks like solder feathering out onto pad and lead with a shiny (tin-lead) or satin (many lead-free) fillet. Balling up on dirty metal means more heat/flux/cleaning — not more brute force.
Rosin fluxes may leave amber residue; some "no-clean" fluxes are meant to stay. Water-soluble fluxes must be cleaned — conductive residue causes leakage and corrosion.
Never use plumber's acid flux on electronics. It is corrosive and will ruin boards over time even if the joint looks pretty today.

lessons.title: Good and bad joints
lessons.summary: What to look for under a bright light.

sections.p: Inspect every joint. A good through-hole joint shows a concave or smooth fillet wetting the pad and lead, no cracks, and lead not moving when cooled. Lead-free may look less mirror-like than tin-lead — satin can still be good.
Dull, lumpy, poor wetting — the metals never got properly hot together, or the joint moved while solidifying. Reflow with flux and proper heat.
Pad not covered, or lead barely tacked. Add heat and a little solder — do not blob from afar.
Solder shorting adjacent pads is a bridge — remove with braid or a pump. Huge blobs hide bad wetting underneath; aesthetic excess is not strength.
Charred flux, lifted pads, melted plastic connectors: too much heat. Let the board cool; repair lifted pads with care or scrap the board if traces tear.

lessons.title: ESD awareness
lessons.summary: Static can kill chips before you smell smoke.

sections.p: ESD (electrostatic discharge) is a tiny spark from static charge. You may not feel it, yet MOSFET gates and IC inputs can be damaged. Humidity, flooring and clothing all change risk.
Work on a grounded ESD mat when possible. Wear a wrist strap clipped to ground (through a safety resistor). Handle boards by edges. Store parts in ESD bags/foam — not loose in plastic junk drawers.
Use an ESD-safe iron and grounded workstation. Don't shuffle across carpet then touch bare CMOS pins on a dry winter day.
Through-hole discretes are tougher than fine CMOS. Still, good habits cost little. Assume modern ICs deserve respect.

lessons.title: Desoldering
lessons.summary: Braid, pumps and removing parts whole.

sections.p: Removing solder is part of the craft. Two basic tools: desoldering braid (wick) and a solder sucker (pump). Flux helps both. Warning: boards and pads are easy to wreck with patience-loss and excess heat.
Place fluxed braid on the joint, heat on top of the braid, watch solder wick up, then remove iron and braid together. Do not drag hot braid sideways across pads.
Heat until solder melts, then trigger the pump with the tip at the joint. Cleared holes let through-hole leads exit. Multiple heat cycles need cooling pauses.
For DIP ICs, alternate pins or use clips/hot-air with care. Chip-quic / low-melt alloys can help advanced rework. If a pad lifts, stop and reassess — forcing makes tears worse.

lessons.title: Rework tips
lessons.summary: Fixing mistakes without making new ones.

sections.p: Rework is deliberate repair: remove bridges, replace a wrong resistor, swap a damaged connector. Plan the heat path. Use fresh flux. Support connectors so you do not tear pads when pulling.
Add flux, touch with a clean tip, and draw excess along the row — or use braid. A little solder plus flux often clears bridges better than a dry tip.
Clear each hole, pull the part, clean pads, insert the new part, solder. Verify orientation (diodes, electrolytics, ICs) before soldering all pins.
SMD rework often uses hot air at controlled temperature/flow. Aim evenly, use nozzles that fit, and mind nearby plastic connectors. Practice on scrap first — this is a skill of its own.
A board with shredded pads and lifted vias may cost more in time than a new board. Good judgement is part of rework.
